Family Health

Thrombosed haemorrhoids: a painful anal lump, treatment and recovery

Updated: October 7, 2026

Written and edited by BeMama Authors team: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

A sudden painful lump at the anus may be a thrombosed haemorrhoid, but examination matters. Treatment ranges from comfort and bowel care to a clinician-performed procedure, depending on the diagnosis and severity.

What a thrombosed haemorrhoid is

Haemorrhoidal tissue is a normal part of the anal canal. Problems arise when these vascular cushions become enlarged or symptomatic. Internal haemorrhoids lie within the canal and may bleed or protrude; external haemorrhoids are covered by sensitive skin around the anal opening. Their symptoms and treatments are not identical.

Thrombosis means that a blood clot has formed within the haemorrhoid. An external clot can create a sudden, tender lump, sometimes blue or purple. This local clot is different from a clot in a deep leg vein and is not usually a life-threatening condition. However, a painful anal lump cannot safely be diagnosed from appearance alone, especially if fever or worsening illness is present.

Pain, swelling and bleeding: what to notice

A thrombosed external haemorrhoid can hurt when sitting, walking or opening the bowels. Swelling, itching and a firm lump may accompany the pain. The skin over a clot can sometimes break and bleed. Internal haemorrhoids more commonly cause bright red bleeding without the same intense skin-level pain, although prolapsed or complicated tissue can be painful.

Fever, pus, spreading redness or feeling unwell with anal pain may indicate an abscess or another problem needing prompt care. Heavy or ongoing bleeding, faintness or severe pain requires urgent assessment. Do not assume that all rectal bleeding comes from piles: fissures, inflammation and bowel disease, including cancer, can also cause it.

Why it can happen

Straining with hard stools, constipation, repeated diarrhoea and other changes in bowel habits can contribute to symptoms. Pregnancy and pushing during birth may also increase pressure in the area. Prolonged time sitting on the toilet can make matters worse; long sedentary periods, including travel, may be relevant to the overall pattern.

Low fibre intake, conditions that cause constipation and age-related weakening of supporting tissue can increase the likelihood of haemorrhoid problems. Even so, clinicians cannot always identify why one haemorrhoid develops a clot and another does not. It is common to have an episode without one obvious trigger, and a clot is not evidence that you did something wrong.

How the diagnosis is checked

A clinician asks when the lump and pain started, whether symptoms are improving, and about bleeding, bowel habits, pregnancy, previous treatment and medicines such as blood thinners. Inspection may show an external thrombosis. Depending on comfort and the clinical question, examination can include a lubricated gloved finger or a short viewing instrument called an anoscope.

Further bowel investigation is selected according to symptoms, examination, age, screening history and other risk factors. A flexible sigmoidoscopy examines the lower colon; a colonoscopy examines more of the colon. These tests can identify polyps or another cause of bleeding, but are not automatically required for every external clot. Persistent or unexplained bleeding should not be dismissed because a haemorrhoid was also found.

Early treatment is a choice, not a three-day deadline

Many external thromboses improve with non-operative care as the body absorbs the clot. For severe pain, a clinician may offer an early procedure under local anaesthetic. Excision removes the clot together with the involved overlying tissue. A small incision to evacuate the clot, sometimes called thrombectomy, is a different procedure and may have a different recurrence pattern.

You may hear that treatment works best within the first 48 to 72 hours. The duration and trend of pain help guide the decision, but evidence does not define a universal cutoff. Do not delay seeking help until a deadline or assume nothing can be done after three days. A person already improving may prefer supportive care; persistent severe pain needs reassessment. Never cut, squeeze or drain the lump at home.

Comfort measures while it settles

A warm, shallow bath or sitz bath for about 10 to 15 minutes can soothe the area. Use comfortably warm water, then pat dry rather than rubbing. A cold pack wrapped in a cloth may ease swelling; do not put ice directly on the skin. Keep cleansing gentle and avoid repeated scrubbing or fragranced products that sting.

A pharmacist can advise on a short course of haemorrhoid cream and an appropriate pain medicine. Paracetamol, also called acetaminophen, may help when suitable. Ibuprofen is not appropriate for everyone and should be avoided when haemorrhoids are bleeding unless a clinician directs otherwise. Codeine can worsen constipation. Pregnancy, breastfeeding, ulcers, kidney problems and other medicines affect what is suitable; topical products do not remove the clot itself.

Other procedures treat different haemorrhoid problems

Most people do not need major surgery. Rubber-band ligation is used for selected internal haemorrhoids: a clinician places a small band to cut off the tissue’s blood supply so it shrinks and falls away. It is not a way to treat a painful external clot yourself. The choice depends on the type and severity of the haemorrhoids and response to bowel care.

Excisional haemorrhoidectomy may be considered for substantial external disease or combined internal and external haemorrhoids, including when other measures have failed. It removes tissue and generally involves more recovery than a small office procedure. Stapled haemorrhoidopexy repositions prolapsing internal tissue; it does not address external haemorrhoids. Current ASCRS guidance does not recommend stapling routinely as first-line surgery because of its risk and recurrence profile.

Recovery depends on the treatment and symptom trend

Without an operation, pain often improves before the lump disappears. Improvement may occur over several days, while the swelling can take a few weeks to settle and sometimes leaves a skin tag. A seven-to-ten-day estimate is not a promise for every person. Increasing pain, new fever or persistent troublesome symptoms should prompt another assessment rather than waiting indefinitely.

After excision or haemorrhoidectomy, follow the team’s wound, bowel and pain-care instructions. Return to work, exercise, lifting and driving depends on the procedure and how you are recovering. More extensive surgery can cause significant discomfort, bleeding, infection or difficulty passing urine. Contact the surgical team promptly for inability to urinate, fever, heavy bleeding or worsening pain; do not assume these are routine parts of healing.

Make bowel movements easier and reduce recurrence

Aim for soft, formed stools that pass without straining. Fruit, vegetables, pulses and whole grains provide fibre; increase the amount gradually if your diet is low in it. An intake around 25 to 30 grams daily is a useful example for many adults, although needs vary. A fibre supplement such as psyllium or methylcellulose may help when food alone is insufficient; a pharmacist can also advise on a suitable laxative if needed.

Drink enough fluid for your circumstances, particularly when increasing fibre, while following any heart or kidney-related fluid restriction. Eight glasses is not a universal prescription. Regular activity, responding to the urge to pass stool and limiting time on the toilet can help. Set aside a relaxed opportunity rather than forcing a bowel movement on schedule. Treat persistent diarrhoea or constipation instead of repeatedly treating the lump alone.

Outlook and follow-up

A thrombosed haemorrhoid usually settles, but the pain can be substantial and recurrence is possible. Excision may reduce recurrence compared with some alternatives, without guaranteeing that another episode will never happen. Keep bowel habits and follow-up in the plan even after symptoms improve.

Seek a review if bleeding recurs, the diagnosis is uncertain or a lump remains troublesome. Tell the clinician about weight loss, a lasting change in bowel habit or a family history of bowel cancer if relevant. These details do not mean that a serious diagnosis is inevitable; they help ensure that the symptoms are investigated appropriately rather than automatically attributed to piles.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

A painful anal lump and rectal bleeding need an appropriate assessment.

Selected external thromboses benefit from early excision; there is no rigid three-day deadline for getting help.

Banding and stapling treat selected internal disease and are not interchangeable with external-clot treatment.

How BeMama can help

Note when pain began and whether it is improving. Ask for a clear bowel-care plan and instructions about symptoms that need reassessment.

When to seek help

Seek urgent care for severe pain, fever or pus, heavy bleeding, faintness or inability to pass urine after treatment. Never drain an anal lump yourself.

Evidence notes updated: October 7, 2026

Key takeaways

  • Pain may improve before the lump disappears.
  • Many cases settle without major surgery.
  • Avoid straining and long periods on the toilet.
  • Do not assume every episode of rectal bleeding is a haemorrhoid.

Frequently asked questions

Is this clot the same as a dangerous clot in a leg vein?

No. A haemorrhoidal clot is local and is not usually life-threatening. The diagnosis still needs checking, especially with fever, worsening pain or significant bleeding.

Can I drain the lump myself?

No. Cutting, squeezing or puncturing it can cause injury, bleeding or infection. Only a qualified clinician should perform a procedure.

Is it too late for help after three days?

No. Three days is not a universal treatment cutoff. Persistent severe pain or an uncertain diagnosis still needs assessment.

Does everyone need thrombectomy?

No. Many cases settle with non-operative care. The clinician considers the severity, duration and trend of pain and may discuss excision or another appropriate approach.

Can a rubber band treat an external clot?

Rubber-band ligation is for selected internal haemorrhoids and is performed by a clinician. It is not a home treatment for an external thrombosis.

How long will the lump last?

Pain often improves over days, but the lump can take weeks to settle and may leave a skin tag. Worsening symptoms need review.

Can I take ibuprofen if the haemorrhoid is bleeding?

Do not use it for bleeding haemorrhoids unless a clinician advises it. Ask about an appropriate alternative and assessment of the bleeding.

Will every person with bleeding need a colonoscopy?

No. The decision depends on the history, examination and risk factors. Persistent or unexplained bleeding should still be investigated appropriately.

Does surgery guarantee it will not return?

No. Some procedures reduce recurrence, but none removes the need for bowel care and follow-up when symptoms return.

Should I force myself to open my bowels at the same time daily?

No. A relaxed routine may help, but avoid straining. Respond to the urge, keep stools soft and seek advice for ongoing constipation or diarrhoea.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
